lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: Before a physical test of a regional office, which ROE check would most directly have prevented the Iowa arrests?
options: Confirm that the client controls the building and that any other authority with jurisdiction has agreed or been informed
Use quieter tools
Test only during business hours
Wear company uniforms
explain: The conflict was over who controlled the courthouse and who had been told. Hours and attire matter, but authorisation from every party with control is the foundation.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
question: Which check would most directly test the name 'promotes the token Paris' for a residual-stream latent?
options: Count how often the latent fires
Clamp the latent higher on prompts where it is off and measure whether the probability of ' Paris' rises
Raise its autointerp detection score
Look at its top five activating examples again
explain: The name is a claim about what the latent writes. An intervention measures that causally; activation-based scores and density only describe where it fires. The logit effect suggests it, and the clamp confirms it through the real network.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard
question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
question: A team's refusal vector lowers the average refusal rate on held-out prompts from 60% to 20%. Which extra measurement best tests whether it is reliable?
options: The per-prompt slope of the behavior against the coefficient, and the fraction of prompts with a negative slope
A larger coefficient, to see whether the rate reaches 0%
The same average measured on the prompts used to build the vector
The norm of the vector compared with the residual stream
explain: Tan et al. show averages can hide many inputs that move the wrong way. Per-input slopes reveal that distribution directly. A larger coefficient changes the effect size, not its reliability; building-set scores leak; the norm ratio sets a scale but says nothing about consistency.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: Rerun the toy with B = 7 s instead of 2 s (L still 5 s). Which readings are late or dropped?
options: e6 and e10 late, e12 dropped, exactly as before
No reading is late, and e12 is still dropped
Nothing is late or dropped
Every out-of-order reading is dropped
explain: When e6 arrives, max = 13 so W = 6 < 10: on time. When e10 arrives, max = 22 so W = 15 < 20: on time. e12 arrives with W = 27 - 7 = 20, past 10 + 5 = 15: still dropped. The price: window [0,10) now first fires at processing time 22.5 s (when e9 arrives) instead of 13.4 s.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Why did the Transformer use scaled dot-product scores instead of Bahdanau's additive scores?
options: Both cost about the same in theory, but the dot product runs as one fast matrix multiplication; scaling fixes its weakness at large d_k
Additive scores cannot be trained with gradient descent
Dot products need no learned parameters at all, so the model is smaller
Additive scores only work with RNN hidden states
explain: Section 3.2.1 says the two have similar theoretical complexity and that dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice. Without scaling, additive attention wins for large d_k, so the paper divides by the square root of d_k. The queries and keys are still produced by learned projections.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
question: A model uses RoPE. A query at position 100 and a key at position 97 have score 2.3. The same query and key vectors are placed at positions 1003 and 1000. What is the score?
options: Lower, because RoPE scores decay with absolute position
2.3, because only the offset (3) enters the score
Unpredictable, because angles like 1003 theta wrap around many times
Higher, because later positions get larger rotations
explain: The rotations by 1003 theta and 1000 theta cancel down to a rotation by the offset, exactly as for 100 and 97, so the score is identical. Wrapping is harmless here because only the difference of angles enters. Long-term decay is about the distance between the two tokens, not about where they sit.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
question: Why does the long document C score high under TF-IDF even though it is not more focused on the query?
options: Its IDF values are higher
TF-IDF divides by document length, which favors long documents
C contains both query terms, and TF-IDF only scores documents with all terms
Longer documents have more tokens, so their raw counts are larger for many terms
explain: IDF depends only on the term, not the document. TF-IDF as written does not divide by length at all, and it scores any document with at least one term (A, B and D are scored too). C wins because a 60-token document simply has room for more occurrences.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
question: $f = x y + x$ with $x = 2$, $y = 5$. What is $\partial f / \partial x$?
options: 5, from the product term only
6: the path through the product gives y = 5 and the added x gives 1
1, from the added x only
7, which is x + y
explain: $x$ reaches $f$ by two paths. Through $xy$ the local rate is $y = 5$; through the bare $+ x$ term it is 1. The paths add: $5 + 1 = 6$. Keeping only one path is the fan-out mistake.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation: the chain rule run backward through a graph
question: A model has 1 million parameters. Roughly how many forward evaluations of the loss does a centered finite-difference gradient need, compared with backprop?
options: About 2, the same as backprop
About 2 million, versus one forward plus one backward pass for backprop
About 1000, the square root of the parameter count
Exactly 1 million, versus 1 million backward passes for backprop
explain: Centered differences need two evaluations per parameter, $2 \times 10^6$ forward passes. Reverse-mode differentiation gets the whole gradient of a scalar loss from one forward and one backward pass, which is why finite differences are only used to spot-check gradients.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
question: After `f() { echo 5; return 3; }` and `y=$(f)`, what are y and `$?`?
options: y is 5 and `$?` is 3
y is 3 and `$?` is 0
y is 5 and `$?` is 0
y is 53 and `$?` is 0
explain: Command substitution captures what f prints, 5. The return value is not output; it becomes the exit status, and an assignment whose value came from `$(...)` takes that command's status, 3 (a real bash run printed `y=5 status=3`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A CI step runs `pytest | tee test.log` (tee copies its input to the screen and to a file) and always shows green even when tests fail. What is the minimal fix?
options: Replace `|` with `&&`
Add `set -u`
Add `set -o pipefail` before the command
Redirect with `2>&1` instead of piping
explain: The pipeline's status is tee's, which succeeds. pipefail makes the pipeline report the rightmost non-zero status, so pytest's failure surfaces. `&&` would stop tee from seeing the output stream at all.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: A balanced binary tree holds a vocabulary of $W = 1{,}048{,}576 = 2^{20}$ words at its leaves. How many sigmoid decisions does hierarchical softmax make to score one word?
explain: The path from the root to a leaf in a balanced tree of $2^{20}$ leaves has 20 inner nodes, one sigmoid each, instead of a million dot products. A Huffman tree is not balanced: frequent words get shorter paths and rare words longer ones, which lowers the average cost on real text.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem with a shared unknown or hashed row, or by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams in the next lesson.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
question: Which of these objectives is minimized by an encoder that maps every image to the same vector?
options: Alignment alone, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}$
NT-Xent with in-batch negatives
Uniformity, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{uniform}}$
MoCo's loss with a queue of negatives
explain: A constant encoder puts every positive pair at distance 0, the minimum of alignment. Every loss that includes negatives or a uniformity term penalizes it: NT-Xent costs ln(2N - 1) per row, and uniformity reaches its maximum, 0.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
question: A server runs LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an 80 GB A100 with 2048-token contexts. Ignoring overheads, roughly how many full sequences fit in the KV space?
options: About 31
About 2,048
About 62
Unlimited, KV lives in host memory
explain: Each sequence needs 2048 x 512 KiB = 1 GiB (about 1.07 GB). 66.6 GB / 1.07 GB is about 62. Halving the context doubles how many fit.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
question: In `addq (%rdi,%rcx,8), %rax`, why is rcx multiplied by 8?
options: Because x86-64 has 8 general-purpose registers
Because the loop is unrolled 8 times
Because memory is read in 8-bit units
Because each long is 8 bytes, so element i starts 8 x i bytes after a
explain: Memory is addressed in bytes, and a long is 8 bytes on x86-64 Linux. a[i] therefore lives at address a + 8 x i. The CPU computes that address as part of the instruction (base rdi plus index rcx times scale 8).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
question: Why does a system call use a trap instruction instead of letting the program jump directly to the kernel's code for write?
options: Jumps cannot reach addresses that large
Trap instructions are faster than jumps
The trap switches to kernel mode and enters only at handlers the kernel registered, so a program cannot run arbitrary kernel code with full privileges
The C library has no way to call functions
explain: If user code could jump anywhere into the kernel with privileges, it could skip permission checks. The trap table, set up at boot in kernel mode, fixes the only entry points, and the mode switch happens in hardware as part of the trap.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
question: Why did Llama 3 find the document mask mattered more in long-context training than in standard 8K pretraining?
options: A 128K-token sequence packs many unrelated documents, so a plain causal mask lets tokens attend to far more unrelated text
Document masks make attention cost linear in sequence length
Long sequences do not use an end-of-text token
The document mask is needed for the learning rate to anneal
explain: With longer windows a token can see many more tokens from other documents, which can distract or teach false dependencies. The mask keeps each prediction conditioned on its own document only. It changes which keys are visible, not the asymptotic cost.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
question: After indexing, which statistic for a term equals the length of its postings list?
options: Its collection frequency
Its document frequency
Its largest term frequency
The number of positions stored for it
explain: One posting per document that contains the term, so the list length is df. Collection frequency counts every occurrence, which is the sum of the tf values stored in those postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
question: Why does Lucene add documents by writing new segments instead of inserting postings into existing lists?
options: Segments are needed to compute idf
Postings are compressed contiguous runs, so in-place insertion would mean rewriting them; append-only segments plus background merges avoid that
Each segment can only hold one field
Lucene cannot store more than 128 documents per segment
explain: Compressed, gap-encoded postings cannot absorb an insert cheaply. Writing a fresh small segment is fast, and merges later rewrite several segments into one larger, well-compressed segment. This is the same main plus auxiliary idea from the textbook, generalized to many segments. The 128 is the packed block size, not a segment limit.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: `int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}; int *p = a + 1;` What is `p[2]`?
options: Undefined, p[2] is past the end
The address of a[3]
explain: p[2] means *(p + 2). p points to a[1], so p + 2 points to a[3], which holds 4. It stays in bounds: the last valid element is a[3].

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
question: `point a = { .x = 1, .y = 2 }; point b = a; b.x = 9;` What is a.x now?
options: Undefined behavior
It does not compile, because structs cannot be assigned
explain: Struct assignment copies every member, so b is an independent copy. Changing b.x leaves a.x at 1. To share one object, you would use a pointer: `point *p = &a; p->x = 9;` would change a.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
question: A crash report shows `#0 nth crash.c:18` and `#1 main crash.c:27`. Which statement is right?
options: main crashed, and nth was the last function it called
The bug must be on line 18, because frame #0 is always the culprit
Line 27 ran after line 18
The crash happened in nth at line 18, called from main at line 27; the cause may be in either
explain: Frame #0 is where execution stopped and #1 is its caller. The faulting line is where the bad pointer was used, not necessarily where the mistake was made: here main passed an index that was out of range.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: Which snippet compiles?
options: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s; a.push('x'); b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; s.push('x'); println!("{a}");`
`let a = &mut s; a.push('x'); let b = &mut s; b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}{b}");`
explain: In option 3, `a` is last used before `b` is created, so the two mutable borrows do not overlap. Option 1 is E0499 (two live `&mut`). Options 2 and 4 are E0502 (a shared borrow is still used after a mutable one starts).

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
question: Does `String` satisfy the bound `T: 'static`?
options: No: only string literals are `'static`
Yes: it owns its data and holds no borrows, even though it is dropped at the end of its scope
Only if it is created at the top of `main`
Only after it is wrapped in a `Box`
explain: A `'static` bound asks that the type contain no short-lived references. Owned data always passes it. Being `'static` as a bound says nothing about how long a particular value lives; the String is still dropped by its owner.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the angle between them?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
45 degrees
It depends on their dimension
explain: For unit vectors the dot product equals $\cos\theta$, and the cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5. The formula holds in any dimension, because any two vectors lie in one flat plane (the plane of all their combinations), and the angle is measured inside it.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
question: For which matrix does $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ have exactly one solution for every $\mathbf{b}$?
explain: The determinants are $4 - 4 = 0$, $10 - 12 = -2$, $6 - 6 = 0$ and $0 - 0 = 0$. Only the second is nonzero, so only it is invertible. A negative determinant is fine: it means the map flips orientation, not that it loses information.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
question: An `nn.Linear(in_features=768, out_features=3072)` receives a batch of 32 token vectors, shape $32 \times 768$. What are the weight shape and the output shape?
options: Weight 3072 x 768, output 32 x 3072
Weight 768 x 3072, output 32 x 768
Weight 3072 x 768, output 3072 x 32
Weight 32 x 3072, output 32 x 3072
explain: PyTorch stores the weight as (out_features, in_features) = $3072\times768$ and computes $XW^\top$: $(32\times768)(768\times3072) = 32\times3072$. The batch size never appears in the weight.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches: noisy gradients and the training loop
question: A training set is stored sorted by label: all cats first, then all dogs. You take minibatches in that order without shuffling. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, since every example is still used once per epoch
The loss becomes non-differentiable
Each minibatch contains a single class, so consecutive gradients pull the model back and forth instead of estimating the full gradient
The learning rate becomes effectively zero
explain: A minibatch gradient is a good estimate only if the batch is a random sample. All-cat batches push toward 'always cat', then all-dog batches push the other way. Shuffling once per epoch fixes it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Early stopping and why big models still generalize
question: In the degree-9 run, why does held-out error start rising again after about 31,000 steps?
options: The learning rate becomes too large late in training
Gradient descent starts fitting directions that hold mostly noise
The Hessian changes during training
The training loss starts increasing
explain: By then the smooth, signal-carrying directions are fitted. Further progress comes from flatter directions, where the targets' components are mostly noise, so the fit gets better on training points and worse elsewhere. For a linear-in-parameters model the Hessian is fixed, and training loss keeps falling throughout.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Build it: a complete training loop in NumPy
question: A teammate computes mu and sd on all 600 rows instead of the training rows. The test precision barely changes. Why is it still a bug?
options: It is not a bug, since the effect is small
It makes training slower
It changes the decision threshold
Test rows influenced the model, so the test score is no longer a clean estimate; on other data or steps the leak can be large
explain: Preprocessing fit on held-out rows is leakage (lesson 11). For a mean and standard deviation on 600 similar rows the effect happens to be small, but the test score is no longer computed on data the pipeline never saw, and the same habit with feature selection inflated accuracy from 0.48 to 0.87.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
question: A hidden unit receives input $x_k = 0$ for this example. What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the weight from $x_k$ into that unit, for this example?
options: Equal to the unit's error delta
0, because BP4 multiplies the error by the input activation
Undefined
The same as the bias gradient
explain: BP4: $\partial L/\partial W_{jk} = a_k \delta_j$. If the input on that edge is 0, the weight had no effect on the output for this example, so its gradient is 0. The bias of the unit still gets $\delta_j$.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Build it: a tiny autograd engine from scratch
question: You add a `relu` method to `Value` with `out = Value(max(0, self.data), (self,))`. Which closure is correct?
options: `self.grad = out.grad`
`self.grad += out.grad`
`self.grad += (self.data > 0) * out.grad`
`self.grad += max(0, out.grad)`
explain: ReLU is the max gate: it passes the upstream gradient when the input was positive and blocks it otherwise, and like every rule it must accumulate with `+=`. micrograd's own relu uses the same test on its output, `(out.data > 0) * out.grad`. Option 4 clips the *gradient*, which is a different (wrong) operation.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
question: Why does a multi-level page table make a TLB miss more expensive than a linear page table?
options: The TLB must be flushed after each lookup
The walk needs a load from the page directory and then from the page of PTEs, instead of one load
Multi-level tables are stored on disk
Each level must be translated by the TLB first
explain: A linear table needs one memory reference to fetch the PTE. A two-level table first reads the page directory entry to find the right page of the page table, then reads the PTE: two loads. It is a time-space trade-off; on a TLB hit the cost is identical.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
question: Why does `pthread_cond_wait` take the mutex as an argument?
options: So it can release the mutex and put the thread to sleep as one atomic step, then re-acquire it before returning
So the woken thread is guaranteed to run before any other thread
Because condition variables are implemented as mutexes
So it can free the mutex permanently once the condition is true
explain: If the thread released the mutex itself and then slept, a signal could arrive in the gap and be lost. Doing both atomically closes that window. Waking does not guarantee running first: that would be Hoare semantics, and pthreads uses Mesa semantics.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
question: An inode has 12 direct pointers and one indirect pointer; blocks are 4 KB and disk addresses 4 bytes. What is the largest file it can describe?
options: 48 KB
4 MB exactly
4 GB
explain: The indirect block holds 4096 / 4 = 1024 pointers. Together with the 12 direct ones that is 1036 blocks of 4 KB = 4144 KB. 48 KB is only the direct part; 4 GB needs a double indirect pointer.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
question: Which change most increases P(sick | positive) for a disease with a 1% base rate, starting from sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09?
options: Raise sensitivity to 0.99
Lower the false positive rate to 0.01
Both help equally
Neither, the base rate fixes the answer
explain: Raising sensitivity takes the posterior from 9.2% to about 10%. Lowering the false positive rate to 0.01 takes it to about 48%, because false positives come from the 99% healthy group and dominate the positives.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
question: Two features have variances 9 and 4 and covariance 3. What is their correlation?
options: 3, the covariance itself
About 0.083, which is 3 / (9 x 4)
0.5, which is 3 / (3 x 2)
explain: Divide the covariance by both standard deviations, the square roots of the variances: 3 / (3 x 2) = 0.5. Dividing by the variances themselves is a common slip.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
question: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for a lift in click rate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new variant is not better
There is a 97% chance the lift is real
If there were no true difference, a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time
The lift is large enough to matter for the business
explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true: it is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data). Getting the probability that the variant is better needs a prior and Bayes' rule. And p says nothing about whether the effect size matters.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: Under Chinchilla-style scaling (N and D each proportional to about $C^{0.5}$), your compute budget grows 10x. How should the model size change?
options: Grow about 10x, keeping tokens fixed
Grow about 5.4x
Grow about 3.2x, and tokens about 3.2x too
Stay fixed and train 10x longer
explain: $10^{0.5} \approx 3.16$ for both N and D, and $3.16 \times 3.16 = 10$ recovers the 10x compute. 5.4x is the Kaplan prescription ($10^{0.73}$) from lesson 5. Putting all of it into one knob walks up a wall of the IsoFLOP valley.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Batch size, learning rate and data limits as you scale
question: Early in a run the loss is 4.0; later it is 2.5. By Kaplan's fit, how did the critical batch size change, and what does that suggest?
options: It stayed fixed, because it depends only on model size
It fell, because a better model has smaller gradients and needs smaller batches
It doubled once, from 0.27M to 0.54M tokens
It grew about 9x (0.27M to 2.55M tokens), so a batch that suits late training wastes tokens early
explain: $B_{crit} \approx 2\times10^8/L^{1/0.21}$ tokens gives 0.27M at 4.0 and 2.55M at 2.5. It depends on the loss, not directly on size: as the true gradient shrinks relative to its noise, bigger batches stay useful. Hence the batch ramps in GPT-3 and Llama 3.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size
question: You will store 10 million passages as 384-dimensional float32 vectors. Roughly how much memory do the raw vectors need?
options: 1.5 GB
3.8 GB
explain: 10,000,000 x 384 x 4 bytes = 15,360,000,000 bytes, about 15.4 GB, before any index overhead such as HNSW graph links. 3.8 GB would be 1 byte per dimension; 30.7 GB would be 768 dimensions.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
question: Encode newer with the 10 toy merges. What comes out?
options: new e r _
new er_
n e w e r _
ne w e r _
explain: Pairs present at the start: (n,e) rank 6, (e,w) and others unranked. Merge (n,e), then (ne,w) rank 7 gives new. Remaining pairs (new,e), (e,r), (r,_) are not in the list, so the result is new e r _. No er_ token was learned.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: Your model is weak at multi-digit addition, and you are designing the tokenizer for its successor. Which change most directly targets the problem?
options: Double the vocabulary so more numbers become single tokens
Remove the end-of-text token
Make numbers tokenize consistently, for example one token per digit as LLaMA does
Switch from UTF-8 to UTF-16 bytes
explain: The problem is that the same digits land in different token groupings depending on what BPE happened to merge. Splitting digits individually (LLaMA) or into fixed-size groups (cl100k) gives a consistent structure. A bigger vocabulary makes more numbers single opaque tokens, which hides their digits from the model.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
question: You stack 100 residual blocks with He-initialized branches and see the activation scale grow about 1.4x per block at init. What is the standard fix?
options: Replace every identity shortcut with a learned projection
Lower the learning rate by 100x
Initialize the last layer (or last BatchNorm gamma) of each branch to zero, so every block starts as the identity
Remove the ReLU from each branch
explain: Adding a branch output about as large as the input doubles the variance, so the scale grows by sqrt 2 per block. Zero-initializing the branch's last scale makes F(x) = 0 at the start; Goyal et al. do this with the last BatchNorm gamma. A lower learning rate does not change the forward pass at init.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
question: You validate a model with BatchNorm but forget `model.eval()`. Validation accuracy changes when you change the validation batch size. Why?
options: Dropout is still active and BatchNorm is unaffected
The running averages are reset at every forward pass
Gradients are being computed during validation
BatchNorm normalizes with each validation batch's own statistics, so each prediction depends on the other examples in its batch
explain: In train mode BatchNorm uses the current batch mean and variance, so changing the batch composition or size changes each example's output. It also keeps updating the running statistics with validation data. In eval mode it uses the fixed running averages.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Instrumenting a run: gradient norms, update ratios, activation stats
question: You resume a crashed AdamW run from a checkpoint that contains only `model.state_dict()`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: AdamW keeps no state between steps
The weights are reloaded in fp16
Gradients from before the crash are added to the first new step
Adam's m and v, its step count and the schedule all restart, so the first steps behave like the start of a new run
explain: Adam's state lives in the optimizer's state_dict and the schedule's position in the scheduler's. Without them the moment estimates restart at zero and warmup starts over, a different trajectory from the one you interrupted.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes), at some accuracy cost. A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: Why does moving internal packages under an npm scope such as @acme defeat dependency confusion?
options: npm refuses to publish scoped packages publicly
A scope maps to exactly one registry, so the resolver never asks the public registry for @acme packages
Scoped names are encrypted
Scoped packages cannot have install scripts
explain: npm's documentation: scopes have a many-to-one relationship with registries; a scope only ever points to one registry. The public registry is simply not consulted for that name. (Also claim the @acme scope publicly so nobody else can.)

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: Codecov's attacker never touched Codecov's git repository. Why didn't that protect anyone?
options: The attacker deleted the repository
Customers downloaded the script from a storage bucket at run time, so the bucket was the real source of truth
GitHub was also compromised
Git repositories cannot store shell scripts
explain: What runs is what is downloaded, not what is in git. The customer who compared the downloaded script with the published hash checked the right thing.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
question: Which attack does SLSA Build L3 provenance NOT protect against?
options: A compromised build step forging the provenance
Modifying an artifact after the build
Uploading a locally built package by hand
A maintainer committing a backdoor to the main branch, which is then built normally
explain: The build was faithful to the source; the source was bad. That needs the Source track (enforced review) and human scrutiny, which is exactly the xz problem.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils II: where the payload hid and how it was caught
question: Which distribution practice would have kept the backdoor out of a package even if the 5.6.1 version was adopted?
options: Verifying the maintainer's signature on the tarball
Running the package's test suite
Building the package from the tagged git source instead of the release tarball
Using a newer compiler
explain: The trigger lived only in the tarball. Arch Linux switched xz to build from git when the backdoor was disclosed. The signature was valid (Jia Tan signed it), and the tests passed.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
question: Over five rounds of a synthetic data loop, distinct-2 of the generated set stays near 0.7, but coverage of the rare slice of a held-out real set falls from 0.5 to 0.2. What is the best reading?
options: The generator is fine: distinct-2 is stable, so diversity is preserved
The held-out real set is too small to trust, so ignore it
Diversity is improving, because rare-slice coverage is supposed to fall as quality rises
The phrasing stays varied but rare content is disappearing: the early-collapse signature of losing the tails
explain: distinct-n measures variety inside the generated set, not whether it still covers the real distribution. Falling rare-slice coverage is exactly the tail loss of lessons 1 and 3, which internal metrics can miss.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Synthetic data at scale: rephrasing, textbooks, reward-filtered SFT
question: A synthetic textbook includes a reworded version of a test question from MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, a 57-subject benchmark). Your decontamination uses 10-gram overlap followed by a SequenceMatcher check. What happens, and what is the sturdier defense?
options: It is caught, because SequenceMatcher compares every sample with every benchmark item
It is caught, because rewording keeps most 10-word runs intact
It does not matter, since contamination only affects pretraining data, not synthetic data
It slips through, since no 10-word run is shared; keep a protected in-house evaluation set the generator never saw
explain: The 10-gram step decides which samples are compared at all, so a paraphrase with no shared 10-gram is never checked. Liu et al. note exactly this gap and recommend safeguarded private benchmarks.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
question: A program grows a 1 GiB mapping with mremap(p, 1 GiB, 2 GiB, MREMAP_MAYMOVE) and keeps using a pointer it saved earlier, q = p + 4096. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: mremap always grows a mapping in place
If the kernel moved the mapping, q points into the old, now unmapped range, so using it can fault
The first 1 GiB is copied byte by byte, so q sees stale data
mremap fails because MREMAP_MAYMOVE only works on file mappings
explain: With MREMAP_MAYMOVE the kernel may relocate the mapping when there is no room to grow in place, and mremap(2) warns that absolute pointers into the old location become invalid. Use the returned address, or store offsets from the start instead of raw pointers.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
question: Eight worker processes each need read-only access to the same 2 GiB lookup table on a machine with 64 GiB of RAM. Which approach uses the least memory?
options: Each worker mmaps the file with PROT_READ
Each worker reads the file into its own malloc buffer
Each worker mmaps with MAP_ANONYMOUS and copies the file in
One worker reads it and sends it to the others over a pipe
explain: Read-only file mappings in all eight workers point at the same page cache pages, so the table occupies about 2 GiB once. Reading into private buffers keeps eight copies (16 GiB) plus the page cache copy. Anonymous memory is private per process too. This read-mostly, fits-in-RAM, shared case is where mmap clearly wins.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Taming the tail: hedged requests and honest reporting
question: A colleague says: 'Our load test with wrk2 at 5,000 requests per second shows p99 = 900 ms but production p99 at the same traffic is 20 ms, so wrk2 must be broken.' What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: HdrHistogram rounds values up by 45x
Production percentiles are always lower than test percentiles
wrk2 sends requests twice
wrk2 measures from intended send times, so if the server cannot sustain 5,000 req/s, queueing builds up and is honestly reported; check that the achieved rate matched the target
explain: If the requested rate exceeds what the system can serve, the backlog grows during the run and every request's latency since its intended time keeps rising. Compare the reported Requests/sec to the -R target and check the test setup (for example, one client machine as bottleneck) before blaming the tool.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
question: Your query parser receives *candidates with 3+ years at their current company*. Which output should the LLM produce?
options: `{"min_years": 3}` with the filter applied to total experience
`{"current_role_min_tenure": "P3Y"}`, leaving the date math to the engine
A list of matching candidate IDs it reasoned out from the resumes
`{"start_before": "2023-10-20"}` computed from its own idea of today
explain: The model's job is to capture meaning as structure: tenure in the current role, at least three years, as an ISO 8601 duration. The engine then finds roles containing the reference date and checks their length. Option 4 bakes in a date the model guessed; option 1 loses the current-company scope.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
question: On a benchmark, majority-vote accuracy rises from 1 to 5 calls and then falls steadily up to 101 calls. Which explanation fits Chen et al.'s analysis?
options: The benchmark mixes queries whose most likely answer is correct, which saturate early, with queries whose most likely answer is wrong, which keep sliding toward 0
Samples become correlated when K is large
Ties are broken in favor of wrong answers
The temperature rises with K
explain: Voting converges to the mode of each query's answer distribution. Easy queries gain until they hit 100% and then stop contributing; hard queries lose with every extra call, so the average eventually turns down.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: A chatbot will serve far more tokens than its pretraining corpus (R much greater than 1), and many prompts are hard for the current model. What does the evidence favor?
options: Investing in a larger or better-trained model
A large per-query test-time budget on the current small model
Majority voting with 10,000 samples
Lookahead search with a PRM
explain: With large R the FLOPs-matched test-time budget shrinks toward M, and on hard questions Snell et al. found additional pretraining more effective than test-time compute.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Making TTT fast: mini-batch gradient descent and the dual form
question: You raise the TTT mini-batch size from 16 to 2048 in a TTT-Linear language model and change nothing else. What do you expect?
options: Lower perplexity, because larger batches give less noisy gradients
No change in quality; b is purely a speed knob because the dual form is exact
Faster training per step but worse perplexity, since the inner loop now takes far fewer real steps (b = T is batch GD, close to linear attention)
Slower training and better perplexity
explain: The dual form is exact for a given b, but b itself changes the algorithm. The TTT paper's ablation shows smaller b improves perplexity because W takes more gradient steps; b = T collapses to batch GD. LaCT gets away with huge chunks only by adding sliding-window attention, wider nonlinear fast weights and a different update rule.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In MAG with a window of 4, the model must answer a question about a name that appeared in token 1 while it is at token 12. Which path can carry the name?
options: The sliding-window attention, because the persistent tokens extend its window
Neither: MAG can only use the last 4 tokens
Only the neural memory branch, which has been trained on every token so far
The gate, which stores the earliest tokens separately
explain: The window covers x9 to x12, and persistent tokens are fixed learned vectors that know nothing about this input. The memory branch has taken a gradient step on every token from x1 on, so it is the only route, and it carries x1 only as well as the memory stored it.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
question: Why does a magazine store an array of pointers instead of threading a linked list through the free objects themselves?
options: Arrays are always faster to traverse than linked lists
Writing a link into a free object would destroy its constructed state, and some managed resources are not writable memory
Linked lists cannot be used as stacks
The depot needs to sort the objects by address
explain: Object caches keep free objects in their constructed state (locks initialized, fields set). A freelist link would clobber part of the object. And the slab and magazine code also manage non-memory resources, where there is nowhere to store a link.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: What threat hunting is, and the hunt that started at 75 cents
question: Stoll's first clue was an accounting program that could not balance its books. In today's terms, what kind of signal was it?
options: A honeypot alert
An anomaly in operational data that no security tool was watching
An indicator of compromise from a threat-intelligence feed
An intrusion detection alert that was correctly triaged
explain: No security control fired. A business system's data was slightly wrong, and someone asked why. Many hunts still start this way: a number that does not add up, a log source that changed volume, a host that behaves unlike its peers. The honeypot (bait files) came later in Stoll's investigation, as a tool to keep the intruder connected.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Baselines: describing normal before hunting the abnormal
question: PEAK suggests scoping a baseline hunt to about 30 to 90 days and to groups of similar systems. What goes wrong if you baseline all 4,000 machines (servers, laptops, domain controllers) as one group?
options: Nothing; more data always gives a better baseline
The query will time out
Behaviour normal for one role looks abnormal for another, so the outliers are mostly role differences, and real outliers within a role are hidden
Baselines must always cover exactly one machine
explain: A domain controller and a laptop do different things. Mixed together, the 'outliers' are mostly servers looking unlike laptops, and a laptop doing something server-like is averaged away. Grouping similar systems is the scoping step PEAK names explicitly.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
question: Why can 'connection to an IP with no DNS lookup' produce false positives?
options: DNS logs never record lookups
Attackers always use DNS
Some legitimate software connects to hard-coded addresses, and lookups made through a different resolver or cached long before the window will be missing
Zeek cannot see IP addresses
explain: The hunt only proves that your DNS logs have no matching answer in your window. Hard-coded addresses in legitimate software, DNS answers cached before the window, and resolvers you do not log all produce the same pattern. Treat it as a lead to combine with rarity, timing and process.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
question: By NIST SP 800-150's definitions, which of these is threat *intelligence* rather than threat information?
options: A list of 500 SHA-256 hashes from a malware repository
The subject line of a phishing email
An assessment that a ransomware group is exploiting the VPN model your firm runs, with a recommended patch deadline
A firewall log line showing a blocked connection
explain: NIST defines threat intelligence as threat information that has been aggregated, analysed, interpreted or enriched to give context for decision-making. Hashes, subject lines and log lines are indicators or observables: useful inputs, but nobody has yet said what they mean for you or what to do.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
question: Four vendor reports state that a domain belongs to the same actor. You find that all four cite one researcher's blog post. How should the credibility grade treat them?
options: As four independent confirmations: grade 1
As grade 5, because repeated claims are improbable
As one source: the four reports add reach, not independent confirmation
Grades only apply to human sources, not reports
explain: Credibility 1 needs independent confirmation. Four reports repeating one original observation are circular reporting: the evidence base is still one blog post, so grade the original claim on its own merits.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph
question: Which properties must every STIX 2.1 Indicator have in addition to the common ones (type, spec_version, id, created, modified)?
options: name and description
confidence and labels
pattern, pattern_type and valid_from
kill_chain_phases
explain: The specification marks pattern, pattern_type and valid_from as required for Indicator. name and description are optional (producers SHOULD provide them), and confidence is an optional common property.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Reading an intelligence product: CISA AA24-038A on Volt Typhoon
question: Which sentence from a summary for the board best preserves the advisory's meaning?
options: China has hacked all US water utilities.
A virus might be in our network.
US agencies, allies co-signing, assess with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored group is pre-positioning in critical infrastructure IT, including water, to enable disruption in a crisis.
We are certainly compromised and must shut down.
explain: It keeps the actor, the sponsor, the confidence level, the sector scope and the purpose, without inflating 'multiple organisations' to 'all' or turning an assessment into certainty about your own network.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
question: Which of these is NOT part of a web app's attack surface?
options: A webhook URL that a payment provider calls
A source code comment explaining a sorting algorithm
A support agent's login to the admin console
A file upload form
explain: A comment is not a point where an attacker can enter, affect, or extract data. Webhooks, privileged logins and upload forms are all entry points.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
question: A team accepts a threat and closes the ticket with no notes. What is wrong?
options: Accept is not a valid response
Accepted threats must be transferred to an insurer
Accepted threats must be scored with DREAD first
Acceptance should be explicit and recorded with the reason, so it can be revisited when the system changes
explain: Accept is a legitimate response, but an unrecorded acceptance is indistinguishable from forgetting. The OWASP cheat sheet asks teams to document each response and why remaining risk is accepted.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Defence in depth and zero trust
question: Which change best reflects NIST's zero trust tenets for an internal wiki?
options: Move the wiki deeper inside the VPN (virtual private network, the encrypted tunnel into the office network)
Add a second firewall in front of the wiki
Allow access only from office IP addresses
Require an authenticated session and a healthy managed device on every request, regardless of network
explain: Zero trust grants access per session based on identity and device state, not location. The other three still trust network position.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Demotion: reclaim that migrates instead of swapping
question: With demotion enabled, reclaim on the DRAM node selects an inactive anonymous page and the CXL node has free space. What happens to the page?
options: It is compressed into zswap first, then moved to CXL
It is migrated to the CXL node and stays mapped; the process can still read it with a normal load
It is written to the swap device and its CXL copy is kept as a cache
It is dropped and re-read from disk on the next access
explain: Demotion is a page migration: same contents, new physical frame on the lower tier, page tables updated. Only if migration fails does the page fall back to ordinary reclaim (swap or zswap).

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Holt-Winters and ARIMA: models with trend and season
question: A product's monthly seasonal swing is about 10 units when sales are 100, and about 50 units when sales are 500. Which Holt-Winters variant fits best?
options: Additive seasonality
No seasonal component, with a damped trend
Multiplicative seasonality
Seasonal naive with a 6-month period
explain: The seasonal swing scales with the level (10 percent of sales), which is the case FPP3 gives for the multiplicative method. Additive seasonality assumes a constant swing in absolute units.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The key schedule: one shared secret, many keys
question: Client and server compute the same (EC)DHE secret, but a middlebox altered one extension in the ClientHello in transit. What happens?
options: Nothing; extensions are not covered by the keys
Only the application keys differ, so the handshake completes and then data fails
The server's certificate is rejected
The handshake keys differ because they include the transcript hash, so decryption or the Finished check fails
explain: The handshake traffic secrets already include Hash(ClientHello..ServerHello). The two sides saw different ClientHellos, so they derive different keys and the first encrypted message fails to decrypt.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
question: A certificate has `Basic Constraints: CA:FALSE` and `Key Usage: Digital Signature`. Its owner uses its key to sign another certificate for `bank.example`. What should a client do with the new certificate?
options: Trust it, because it chains to a trusted root
Trust it only if bank.example is in the original SAN
Reject it: the issuer is marked as not a CA and lacks keyCertSign, so it may not issue certificates
Ask the user
explain: Basic Constraints and Key Usage exist exactly to stop leaf certificates acting as CAs. Path validation must check them on every issuer in the chain; skipping that check is a classic bug class.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: When CAs fail: DigiNotar, Symantec and an expired root
question: A CA in some other country, which your company never uses, is compromised and issues a certificate for your domain. Why are your users at risk?
options: They are not, because your certificate is from a different CA
Because CAs share private keys
Only if your CAA record allows that CA
Because browsers accept a certificate from any trusted CA for any domain unless something else (pinning, CT enforcement, distrust) stops it
explain: The Web PKI has no built-in link between a domain and its CA. CAA only instructs honest CAs at issuance time; a compromised CA ignores it. CT logging requirements and monitoring are what make such certificates visible.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
question: Why should a company's internal root CA include a name constraints extension?
options: So that if the CA or one of its subordinates is misused, it cannot issue certificates trusted for names outside the company's domains, such as public banking sites
To make certificates smaller
Because public CAs require it
To enable mTLS
explain: Every machine that installs the root trusts what it signs. Name constraints cap that trust to the names you actually own, which limits the damage of a compromise. OpenSSL rejected the out-of-scope certificate with a permitted subtree violation.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
question: A teammate moves a fused kernel from CUDA to Triton. Which of these do they still have to decide themselves in Triton?
options: Where to put __syncthreads() barriers between shared memory writes and reads
How large a tile each program instance processes and how the grid maps to tiles
Which thread in a warp loads which address so loads are coalesced
How much shared memory to allocate for staging operand tiles
explain: Tile sizes and the program-to-tile mapping are the programmer's job in Triton (often with the autotuner's help). Barriers, coalescing and shared memory allocation are listed in the Triton docs as things the compiler handles automatically.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
question: A matmul config with BLOCK 128 x 256 x 64 in fp16 is extended from num_stages=3 to num_stages=6. Using the simplified estimate, what is the most likely result on a compute capability 9.0 GPU (228 KB of shared memory per SM, at most 227 KB per thread block)?
options: A 2x speedup because twice as many loads overlap
No change, because num_stages only affects registers
It needs about 288 KiB of operand buffers, more than the SM has, so the config fails to launch or is unusable
The compiler automatically shrinks the tiles to fit
explain: 6 x 49,152 bytes = 294,912 bytes (288 KiB) of operand buffers, beyond the 227 KB a thread block may use on compute capability 9.0. Even when stages fit, they help only while there is load latency left to hide; after that they just cost memory.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
question: A Transfusion-style step has L_LM = 0.942 and L_DDPM = 0.07375. What is the total loss with lambda = 5?
explain: 0.942 + 5 x 0.07375 = 0.942 + 0.369 = 1.311. 1.016 is lambda = 1. 4.78 wrongly multiplies the text term by 5 instead (5 x 0.942 + 0.074 is about 4.78).

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
question: A function-as-a-service platform boots a fresh nginx unikernel for each burst of requests and destroys it after a few seconds. Which allocator choice from the Unikraft measurements fits best?
options: A fast-booting allocator such as bootalloc, because boot time dominates a short-lived instance
The buddy allocator, because its throughput at steady state matched TLSF and mimalloc
Any allocator, because allocator choice only affects throughput
mimalloc, because it is always fastest
explain: For just-in-time instances, boot time matters most, and allocator choice moved nginx guest boot from 0.49 ms (bootalloc) to 3.07 ms (buddy). The paper itself says such a use case should avoid the buddy allocator.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: A team ports a UDP service to a unikernel using the standard socket API on lwip, and it is slower than on a Linux VM. Which next step matches the evidence from the Unikraft key-value experiment?
options: Enable binary compatibility to use Linux's network stack
Add more vCPUs, since lwip scales linearly
Code the hot path against the uknetdev driver API in polling mode, bypassing the TCP/IP stack and sockets
Switch the allocator to buddy for better throughput
explain: lwip sockets gave 319 K/s; coding against uknetdev gave 6.3 M/s on one core. Binary compatibility does not bring Linux's network stack into the unikernel, and the evaluated images were single-core.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
question: Squared L2 has intensity 0.75 FLOP per byte and dot product 0.5. On a memory-bound scan, which runs faster per distance?
options: Dot product, because it does fewer FLOPs
About the same, because both read the same 4d bytes
L2, because higher intensity is always faster
Neither can be computed with SIMD
explain: When the limit is bytes, the extra subtract in L2 hides under the memory stall. Both read one 3,072-byte vector per distance, so their throughput is about equal.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
question: Why doesn't HybridFlow simply use a single controller for everything, as classic RL frameworks such as RLlib do?
options: Single controllers cannot express data dependencies between models
Ray does not support GPU workers
Dispatching every operation of a sharded LLM from one central process adds too much overhead; SPMD inside each model avoids it
A single controller forces all models to use the same parallelism
explain: The paper's diagnosis: single-controller frameworks were built for networks of at most hundreds of MB. For LLMs with complex parallelism the central dispatch overhead is too high, so HybridFlow keeps central control only between nodes and lets each node run multi-controller.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Weight handoff: from 3D-HybridEngine to sleep, wake and streaming
question: Which run gains least from `delta_sharded` weight sync?
options: Qwen3-235B-A22B MoE with trainer and rollout on separate nodes
Qwen3-0.6B with trainer and rollout on one NVLink node
Qwen2.5-72B with trainer and rollout on separate nodes
Qwen3-8B with FSDP2 across 2 trainer and 2 rollout nodes
explain: The doc measured 0.59 s versus 0.61 s for the 0.6B model inside one node: a full broadcast is already cheap on a fast local link with a small model. The larger multi-node runs saw about 1.55x to 21x because the full broadcast pays a full-model materialization that grows with size.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Algorithms as config: critics, estimators and rollout correction
question: You switch a working GRPO run to PPO with GAE. Which change in config and resources does that require?
options: Only algorithm.adv_estimator=gae; the actor doubles as the critic
Set rollout.n to at least 2, because GAE needs groups
Disable the reference model, because GAE replaces the KL term
adv_estimator=gae plus a critic group (model path, optimizer, token budget); the critic WorkerGroup needs its own weights and optimizer state and adds the values and update_critic stages
explain: GAE needs value estimates, so verl adds a critic TrainingWorker on the global pool with its own memory and two stages per step. PPO does not need groups (the quickstart uses n = 1), and the KL setting is independent of the estimator.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions
question: Video-ChatGPT keeps T + N tokens by averaging over space and over time separately. Which question is it worst at?
options: What objects appear in the video?
Is the video indoors or outdoors?
Did the person pick up the cup before or after opening the door?
What is the overall topic of the video?
explain: The N spatial tokens are averaged over all frames, and the T temporal tokens are each one averaged vector per frame. Fine spatial detail tied to a specific moment is blurred, which hurts ordering questions about small actions.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Keep S = 256 tokens per frame and double the clip from 16 to 32 frames. What happens to the attention pair counts?
options: Every term doubles, so the ratio stays at 15.1
Spatial pairs double to 2,097,152, temporal pairs quadruple to 262,144, full attention quadruples to 67,108,864
Spatial pairs quadruple and temporal pairs double
Nothing changes because attention is per frame
explain: Spatial is T S squared, linear in T. Temporal is S T squared, quadratic in T but small while T is much less than S. Full is (TS) squared. The ST total is 2,359,296, so the advantage grows to TS/(S+T) = 28.4x.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
question: A team wants to train an RL agent for an Atari game cheaply using imagined experience, and they can collect actions and rewards by playing. Which approach fits best?
options: A model-based RL world model trained on their own action-labelled transitions, such as DreamerV3 or DIAMOND
A Genie-style model trained on unlabelled internet video, since labels are unnecessary
A text-to-video model prompted with the game's name
No world model: imagined experience cannot train agents
explain: When actions and rewards are available, action-conditioned world models built for RL (DreamerV3's latent imagination, DIAMOND's diffusion model with an Atari 100k mean HNS of 1.46) are the direct fit. Genie's latent actions solve a different problem: learning control from video with no labels.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
question: A hospital fine-tunes an ImageNet-21k ViT on 3,000 X-rays from scanner A; it will be deployed on scanner B, which produces visibly different images. Which plan best matches the evidence in this lesson?
options: Full fine-tune with a randomly initialized head, since it has the highest in-distribution accuracy
Train only the position embeddings
LP-FT: fit the head on frozen features first, then fine-tune all layers
Skip training and use the ImageNet head directly
explain: Deployment shift is exactly where Kumar et al. found fine-tuning from a random head loses to probing, and where LP-FT won on 10 of 10 OOD datasets. The ImageNet head predicts ImageNet classes, and position embeddings alone cannot learn new classes.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Why per-step tokens break at 50 Hz, and how FAST compresses them
question: A bimanual robot (14 action dims) runs at 50 Hz. How many tokens does per-step 256-bin tokenization need for a 1-second chunk?
explain: 14 dims x 50 steps = 700 tokens, matching the FAST paper's shirt-folding row. FAST needed about 53 for the same chunk.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
question: In the VQ-VAE loss, which parameters receive gradient from the middle term $\lVert \mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e \rVert^2$?
options: The encoder only
The decoder only
Both the encoder and the codebook
The codebook only
explain: sg blocks the gradient to z_e, so only the codebook vectors e are updated by this term. The paper states: the decoder optimises the first term, the encoder the first and last, and the embeddings the middle term.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Token budgets: bits per image, 1D tokenizers and early fusion
question: You can either double the codebook from 8192 to 16,384 codes or halve the number of image tokens from 1024 to 512. Which choice reduces the stage 2 transformer's attention compute more, and why?
options: Doubling the codebook, because a larger softmax is the dominant cost
They are equivalent, since both change bits per image by the same factor
Halving tokens, because attention pairs scale with the square of sequence length while codebook size adds only one bit per token
Neither changes compute
explain: Halving T cuts attention pairs by 4x and bits per image by 2x. Doubling K adds 1 bit per token (13 to 14) and enlarges the embedding and output layers, but leaves sequence length, and thus attention cost, unchanged.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
question: A model mixes a backend that reports `reorder_batch_threshold = 1` with one that reports `None`. Does the runner reorder?
options: No, because None disables reordering for everyone
Yes, but each backend gets its own differently ordered copy of the batch
Yes, with threshold 1. The runner takes the minimum and ignores None
Only on steps that contain no prefills
explain: `calculate_reorder_batch_threshold` reduces with a min that skips None. One batch order is shared by all layers, so the smallest threshold wins, and backends that need no order are unaffected.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
question: Qwen2-VL's model card says the default visual-token range is 4 to 16,384 per image and suggests setting max_pixels to 1280 x 28 x 28 to save memory. What happens to a 12-megapixel phone photo under that setting?
options: It is resized, keeping its aspect ratio, so that it fits the pixel budget, and costs about 1,230 tokens instead of about 15,500
It is rejected because it exceeds max_pixels
It is cut into 336 x 336 tiles and every tile is kept
Nothing changes because Qwen2-VL uses native resolution
explain: The resize rule scales the image down, preserving aspect ratio, until it fits within max_pixels, then rounds each side to a multiple of 28. A 3024 x 4032 photo becomes 840 x 1148: 1,230 merged tokens plus 2 markers. Native resolution only holds inside the configured pixel range.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
